claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response of high-entropy alloys is governed by the dynamic integrity of a passivating spinel-type oxide film.
The passivating spinel-type film forms in situ through surface enrichment in oxide-forming elements such as Al and Fe.
A robust oxide film resists mechanical removal during sliding.
The oxide film limits ion transport or metal-solution contact and thereby passivates corrosion.
MgAlTiVFeCo- or AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5-type high-entropy alloys can develop protective surface oxides as a consequence of high-temperature processing.
Ambient or slightly elevated tribo-corrosion temperatures provide active oxide-film formation kinetics.
The relevant structural mediator is a dense, continuous spinel-type oxide film that acts as both a mechanical barrier and an electrochemical passivation layer.
Sliding wear intermittently abrades the protective oxide film.
High-temperature processing produces a sufficiently robust and oxide-former-enriched surface for rapid re-establishment of a continuous film after abrasion.
The balance between mechanical film removal and electrochemical repassivation governs overall tribo-corrosion degradation.
A robust-film specimen will have a lower corrosion current density than a lower-temperature-processed baseline with a less-developed film.
A robust-film specimen will have a lower wear depth than the matched baseline.
Simultaneously reducing corrosion current and wear depth will reduce total coupled degradation.
Lower-temperature or alternative processing produces a less-developed or heterogeneous passive film suitable as the baseline.
The predicted protection holds when film regeneration is fast enough to offset removal under moderate wear loads.
The protection may fail at very high mechanical loads or in environments where the oxide is chemically unstable.
